'''''Rosa bracteata''''', commonly known as the '''Macartney rose''', is a species of [[rose]] native to southern China and Taiwan that has become invasive in parts of the United States following its introduction as an ornamental plant. It is the only wild species in the section ''Bracteatae'' of the genus ''Rosa''.<ref name="Li2026">{{cite journal

==Etymology==
''Rosa bracteata'' – ''bracteata'' referring to the notable [[bracts]] below the flowers – is commonly referred to as the '''Macartney rose'''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Macartney Rose |url=http://www.herbiguide.com.au/Descriptions/hg_Macartney_Rose.htm#:~:text=Names%3A,prominent%20bracts%20below%20the%20flowers |website=HerbiGuide |accessdate=5 November 2020}}</ref> Its name links back to a German botanist, [[Johann Christoph Wendland]], who is credited with naming the species.<ref name="IPNI">{{cite web |title=Rosa bracteata J.C.Wendl. |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/731853-1 |website=International Plant Names Index |publisher=The Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Harvard University Herbaria & Libraries and Australian National Botanic Gardens}}</ref> The name ''Macartney rose'' originates from the mid 18th century, when it was named after [[George Macartney, 1st Earl Macartney|George Macartney]], the 1st Earl Macartney in England.<ref>{{cite web |title=Macartney rose |url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/Macartney%20rose |website=Merriam-Webster Dictionary |publisher=Merriam-Webster |accessdate=5 November 2020}}</ref> According to the Global Invasive Species Database, this rose is also referred to by other names – though less commonly – such as the ''Chickasaw rose'' and the ''fragrant white climbing rose'', both of English origin, and ''shuo bao qiang wei'', which is of Chinese origin.<ref>{{cite web |title=issg Database: Ecology of ''Rosa bracteata'' |url=http://issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=1390&fr=1&sts=&lang=EN |website=GLOBAL INVASIVE SPECIES DATABASE |publisher=Invasive Species Specialist Group (ISSG) |accessdate=5 November 2020}}</ref>

==Description== 
The Macartney rose is native to southern China and Taiwan,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:731853-1|title=''Rosa bracteata'' J.C.Wendl.|website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Kew Science |accessdate=10 November 2020}}</ref> but is now considered to be an invasive species across many states in the United States ever since its introduction as an [[ornamental plant]].<ref name="Macartney rose ''Rosa bracteata'' J.C. Wendl.">{{cite web |title=Macartney rose ''Rosa bracteata'' J.C. Wendl. |url=https://www.invasiveplantatlas.org/subject.html?sub=4606 |website=Invasive Plant Atlas of the United States |publisher=National Park Service; University of Georgia Center for Invasive Species and Ecosystem Health |accessdate=4 November 2020}}</ref><ref name="''Rosa bracteata'', Macartney Rose">{{cite web |title=''Rosa bracteata'', Macartney Rose |url=https://invasive-species.extension.org/rosa-bracteata-macartney-rose/ |website=Invasive Species |publisher=Cooperative eXtension System |accessdate=4 November 2020}}</ref><ref name="INVASIVE-SPECIES">{{cite web|title=Invasive Species: ''Rosa bracteata'', Macartney Rose|url=https://invasive-species.extension.org/rosa-bracteata-macartney-rose/#:~:text=Invasive%20Species%3A%20Rosa%20bracteata%2C%20Macartney,throughout%20the%20Southern%20United%20States.&text=Fruit%20are%20small%2C%20green%20to,present%20from%20July%20through%20December|accessdate=3 November 2020|website=Invasive Species |publisher=Cooperative eXtension System}}</ref><ref name="Plants of Texas Rangelands">{{cite web|title=Macartney rose ''Rosa bracteata'' Wendl. Rosaceae|url=https://rangeplants.tamu.edu/plant/macartney-rose/|accessdate=3 November 2020|website=Plants of Texas Rangelands|publisher=Texas A&M AgriLIFE eXtension}}</ref><ref name="PLANTS Database">{{cite web|title=Plant Profile for ''Rosa bracteata'' (Macartney rose)|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=ROBR|access-date=3 November 2020|website=PLANTS Database|publisher=United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) National Resources Conservation Service}}</ref><ref name="Texas Invasives">{{cite web|title=''ROSA BRACTEATA'' MACARTNEY ROSE|url=https://texasinvasives.org/plant_database/detail.php?symbol=ROBR|accessdate=3 November 2020|website=Texas Invasives|publisher=Texas A&M AgriLIFE eXtension}}</ref><ref name="GLOBAL INVASIVE SPECIES DATABASE">{{cite web|title=''Rosa bracteata''|url=http://www.iucngisd.org/gisd/species.php?sc=1390|accessdate=3 November 2020|website=GLOBAL INVASIVE SPECIES DATABASE|publisher=Invasive Species Specialist Group ISSG}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Rosa bracteata'' is a highly adaptable plant and can grow in highly disturbed areas.<ref name="INVASIVE-SPECIES" /><ref name="Plants of Texas Rangelands" /> It can be found in areas ranging from pastures, rangeland, drainage ditches, and along roadsides and fence lines.<ref name="Plants of Texas Rangelands" /> ''R. bracteata'' tends to prefer dark, waterlogged, and clay-based soil compositions.<ref name="ENLOE">{{cite journal |last1=Enloe |first1=S.F. |last2=Kline |first2=W.N. |last3=Aulakh |first3=J.S. |last4=Bethke |first4=R.K. |last5=Gladney |first5=J.B. |last6=Lauer |first6=D.K. |title=Macartney Rose (''Rosa bracteata'') Response to Herbicide and Mowing Treatments |journal=Invasive Plant Science and Management |date=2013 |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=260–267 |doi=10.1614/IPSM-D-12-00049.1 |bibcode=2013IPSM....6..260E |s2cid=86418635 |url=https://doi.org/10.1614/IPSM-D-12-00049.1 |accessdate=4 November 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This species was introduced into the United States from Asia, and is only found within the lower 48 states, mostly in the southeastern United States.<ref name="''Rosa bracteata'', Macartney Rose" /><ref name="PLANTS Database" /> Some of the states it can be found in include Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina, Tennessee, Kentucky, Virginia, and Maryland.<ref name="PLANTS Database" />

Its method of dispersal is through animals, where it is spread by livestock, birds, and other herbivorous organisms. The rose's fruit gets eaten by these animals, which acts as a germination technique after going through the digestive tract of the foraging animal.<ref name ="SCIFRES">{{cite journal |last1=Scifres |first1=C.J. |title=Fall Application of Herbicides Improves Macartney Rose-infest coastal Prairie Rangelands |journal=Rangeland Ecology & Management/Journal of Range Management Archive |date=1975 |volume=28 |issue=6 |pages=483–486 |doi=10.2307/3897229 |jstor=3897229 |hdl=10150/646972 |s2cid=88992928 |url=https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/381b/a9ef0a1e11aa937f48c231aca2bd4d67491f.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200211011956/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/381b/a9ef0a1e11aa937f48c231aca2bd4d67491f.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=2020-02-11 |accessdate=4 November 2020|hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Morphology and ecology==
Rosa bracteata is a perennial evergreen shrub that often forms dense clumps.<ref name="INVASIVE-SPECIES" /><ref name="Plants of Texas Rangelands" /><ref name="PLANTS Database" /> This species of rose can grow up to {{convert|10|ft|m}} in height and width.<ref name="Plants of Texas Rangelands" />

===Leaves and stem===
''Rosa bracteata'' has recurved thorns which are modified leaves all along its stem.<ref name="INVASIVE-SPECIES" /><ref name="Plants of Texas Rangelands" /> Its leaves are serrated and placed in an alternate pattern and range between {{convert|1 and 3|in|cm}} in length; they are [[pinnately]] compound with 5 to 9 thick leaflets per leaf.<ref name="Macartney rose ''Rosa bracteata'' J.C. Wendl." /><ref name="''Rosa bracteata'', Macartney Rose" /><ref name="INVASIVE-SPECIES" /><ref name="Plants of Texas Rangelands" /><ref name="Texas Invasives" /> The tops of the leaves can be described as glossy or shiny as compared to the bottoms of the leaves which are a muted green.<ref name="Plants of Texas Rangelands" />

===Flowers, fruit and seeds===
The flowers of this rose occur in either single or bunched compositions, usually donning five-petaled white flowers of 1–3 in number on bunches of short stalks.<ref name="Macartney rose ''Rosa bracteata'' J.C. Wendl." /><ref name="''Rosa bracteata'', Macartney Rose" /><ref name="INVASIVE-SPECIES" /><ref name="Plants of Texas Rangelands" /> These flowers can typically be seen from April to June which are a part of the spring and summer months in the Northern Hemisphere.<ref name="''Rosa bracteata'', Macartney Rose" /><ref name="INVASIVE-SPECIES" /> Its hips are spherical in shape and are usually a reddish color when ripe.<ref name="Macartney rose ''Rosa bracteata'' J.C. Wendl." /><ref name="''Rosa bracteata'', Macartney Rose" /><ref name="INVASIVE-SPECIES" /><ref name="Plants of Texas Rangelands" /><ref name="Texas Invasives" /> These can be seen from July to December.<ref name="''Rosa bracteata'', Macartney Rose" /><ref name="INVASIVE-SPECIES" />
Its seeds are generally dormant when first created but germinate in temperatures around {{convert|41|°F|°C|abbr=on}}; its optimal temperatures for growth fall between {{convert|68 and 86|°F|°C|abbr=on}}.<ref name="Plants of Louisiana">{{cite web|title=''Rosa bracteata'' Macartney rose|url=https://warcapps.usgs.gov/PlantID/Species/Details/1578|accessdate=3 November 2020|website=Plants of Louisiana|publisher=United States Geological Survey (USGS)}}</ref>

==Genomics==
In 2026, a chromosome-scale genome assembly of ''Rosa bracteata'' was published using long-read sequencing and Hi-C scaffolding technologies. The genome assembly is approximately 540 Mb in length and organized into seven pseudochromosomes, consistent with the species’ diploid chromosome number (2n = 14). The study predicted 42,789 protein-coding genes and reported high assembly completeness.<ref name="Li2026"/>

==Invasive species==
''Rosa bracteata'' has been a major concern as an invasive species for those raising livestock. Infestations of ''Rosa bracteata'' tend to clump together and create thickets that can be up to three meters high which cause issues for movement of livestock and its quick proliferation saps nutrients from surrounding species, stunting their growth.<ref name="SCIFRES" /> When mechanical means of disruption are used, such as mowing, the plant is able to regrow from a shallow root which means that it is very difficult to actually remove the species when it has entered a novel ecosystem.<ref name="ENLOE" /> Fire is similarly ineffective because of this regenerative ability which means extensive research has been done into the usage of herbicides to treat this particular species.<ref name="ENLOE" />

===Herbicide applications===
According to a study done in 2013, the effectiveness of herbicide applications on ''Rosa bracteata'' tend to vary by the timing they are introduced to the organism, for example: all three herbicide treatments of 2,4-D/aminopyralid, aminopyralid/metsulfuron, and picloram/2,4-D all had very effective reduction when treated at the month of October and very poor reduction when applied during May.<ref name="ENLOE" /> In general, there is no singular herbicide or method of mechanical disruption that can effectively deal with ''Rosa bracteata''; efficient pest control employs a multitude of these tools in tandem.<ref>{{cite web |title=How to Manage Macartney Rose |url=https://texnat.tamu.edu/about/brush-busters/macartney-rose/ |website=Texas Natural Resources Server |publisher=Texas A&M Agrilife |accessdate=5 November 2020}}</ref>

==Usage== 
''Rosa bracteata'' was once used in Texas as a "living fence" for livestock grazing, although it was originally introduced from Asia as an [[ornamental plant]].<ref name="INVASIVE-SPECIES" /><ref name="Plants of Texas Rangelands" /><ref name="GLOBAL INVASIVE SPECIES DATABASE" /> It has also had a history of being used for erosion control and has been used for cross-breeding rose [[cultivars]].<ref name="GLOBAL INVASIVE SPECIES DATABASE" />

It is thought that ''Rosa bracteata'' had been used alongside other rose species including ''R. brunonii'', ''[[Rosa foetida|R. foetida]]'', and ''R. eglanteria'' for its medicinal properties in ancient India by infusing it with water and oils, and by making teas. In [[Ayurvedic]] medicine, different rose species (including ''R. bracteata'') were commonly used to cure spiritual ailments like a blockage in the chakras as well as for remedies for fever and acid reflux.<ref name="Indian Rose Federation">{{cite web |title=Indian Rose Federation History |url=https://www.indianrosefederation.com/aboutus.html |website=The Indian Rose Federation |publisher=Indian Rose Federation |accessdate=5 November 2020}}</ref> Roses were also worn in ceremonies, made into perfumes, and were an integral part of everyday life in India among both the elite classes and non-elite ones.<ref name="Indian Rose Federation" />

==History==
This rose species is thought to originate from the Indian subcontinent in the [[Himalayas]], an area rich with mythology, lore and spiritualism. Mentions of ''Rosa bracteata'', or sometimes referred to by other names such as "sivapriya", can be found in scriptures dating back to the 1st century BC. [[Gautama Buddha|Gautama the Buddha]] who is usually depicted meditating on a pedestal of lotuses, can be seen in a few depictions meditating on a pedestal of a five petalled rose resembling ''Rosa bracteata''. Over time, the rose has been mentioned in Chinese history which was facilitated by trade between these regions.<ref name="Indian Rose Federation" />
